An analysis of PM2.5 exposure and independent living need, using public EPA and Census Bureau data | Methodology developed by Genie Tang, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, July 2026

What this work sample demonstrates

Living alone, having a disability, having no vehicle available, and facing a language barrier are four tract-level indicators of potential need for independent living support, and each can also make it harder to avoid or recover from environmental exposure. This project asks where high fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) coincides with tracts that score high on these indicators across California. Tracts where predicted exposure and the need index are both high are places worth investigating for support planning.

Annual PM2.5 observations from the U.S. EPA Air Quality System were combined with American Community Survey census tract indicators describing disability, living alone, vehicle access, and English proficiency. PM2.5 data cover calendar year 2024, and the ACS tract indicators are the 2020-2024 five-year estimates, the most recent tract-level release available when this analysis was prepared.

The need index is a composite of those four measures, each converted to a percentile rank among California tracts and averaged with equal weight. Tracts where a measure could not be computed were excluded before ranking, leaving 9,048 tracts in the analysis.

Monitor locations and variogram

Monitor coverage is denser in the Central Valley and South Coast basins.

Kriged PM2.5 surface

Predicted PM2.5 is highest across the Central Valley and South Coast basin and lowest along the coast and at elevation.

Priority tracts: exposure and need together

1,112 of 9,048 tracts sit in the top tercile of both predicted PM2.5 and the need index.

These tracts mark where high predicted PM2.5 and a high need-index score coincide, a reason to investigate independent living support needs there. This example illustrates a method that could be adapted for the proposed Richmond case study: crossing a predicted exposure surface with population indicators at neighbourhood scale, with built-environment variables added alongside the demographic ones.

A closer look: Contra Costa County

Exposure-and-need categories across Contra Costa County, which includes Richmond.

This matches the broader pattern in this analysis: need runs high in specific Contra Costa tracts, while the highest predicted PM2.5 values occur primarily in the Central Valley and South Coast. It is a useful counterpoint to the statewide priority map above, and illustrates the kind of exposure-and-need crossing the proposed Richmond case study could adapt, at neighbourhood scale and with built-environment variables added.

This is a one-time analysis of a published, publicly available dataset, not a live feed. It uses the same public EPA Air Quality System and American Community Survey sources, and it can be re-run whenever a newer vintage of both is released.
PM2.5 Exposure and Independent Living Need in California, July 2026 | Data sources: U.S. EPA Air Quality System (annual PM2.5 monitor summaries, calendar year 2024) and U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (tract-level disability, living-alone, vehicle-access, and English-proficiency estimates, 2020-2024 five-year estimates) | Method: ordinary kriging with an exponential variogram model, evaluated by ten-fold cross-validation | Public data only | Methodology developed by Genie Tang, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
